text:
In the last days of August 1854, cholera broke out in Soho, a crowded and poor district of London, and within roughly ten days more than five hundred people living within a few hundred yards of the corner of Broad Street and Cambridge Street had died, many of them within a day or two of first falling ill. Cholera was then a disease that struck without warning, producing violent vomiting and diarrhoea that drained the body of water until the skin turned blue and grey and the victim collapsed, and almost nobody in authority doubted what caused it, since the accepted view held that epidemics rose from foul air, the miasma given off by rotting refuse, open sewers and the damp ground of poor neighbourhoods. John Snow, a physician who lived a few streets from the outbreak and who was best known for having made surgery bearable by administering chloroform and ether with unusual precision, had long believed the accepted view was wrong. Years earlier, during the epidemic of 1848 and 1849, he had reasoned that a disease which began in the gut, with symptoms that never touched the lungs, must be swallowed rather than breathed, and that it must travel from the sick to the healthy through something they shared, most plausibly the water supply, which in London at that time was drawn partly from the Thames, into which the city's sewage also drained.

He had already found striking support for this idea in south London, where two water companies supplied houses on the same streets, in the same neighbourhoods and among people of the same incomes, so that a family's water depended only on which company had laid pipes to their door. The Lambeth company had moved its intake upstream of the city's sewage in 1852, while the Southwark and Vauxhall company continued to draw its water from the polluted stretch below, and when Snow went from house to house tallying deaths he found that those served by the downstream company died of cholera at many times the rate of those served by the upstream one, a comparison that worked almost like a deliberate experiment even though nobody had arranged it.

When the Soho outbreak began, Snow therefore had a hypothesis ready and went to the neighbourhood itself to test it. He obtained the register of deaths from the General Register Office and began to visit the families involved, asking where each household got its drinking water, and he plotted every death on a street map, marking each with a short black bar so that the cases piled up along the lines of houses. The bars gathered thickly around the public pump in Broad Street, and the closer a house lay to that pump the more deaths it seemed to have suffered, although Snow was careful to note that the pattern was not a perfect circle and that distance by the walking route to a pump mattered more than distance in a straight line, since people naturally used whichever pump was easiest to reach.

The exceptions told him as much as the rule did. A workhouse on nearby Poland Street, housing more than five hundred inmates, lost only a handful of people, and Snow learned that it had its own well and so had no need of the Broad Street pump, while a brewery on the same street, whose workers were given malt liquor to drink during the day and had their own supply of water too, lost nobody at all. Then there was the case of a widow who lived far away in Hampstead and died of cholera after the outbreak had begun, and when Snow made inquiries he discovered that she had once lived in Soho and liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a carboy of it brought to her house every day, and that her niece, who had drunk some of it too, had died as well, with no other cholera cases anywhere near them.

Convinced, Snow brought his evidence on 7 September to the Board of Guardians of St James's parish, the local body that administered the area, and although the guardians did not understand or fully accept his argument they agreed to remove the handle of the pump the next day, which left the pump unusable and sent residents elsewhere for their water. The outbreak was already falling by then, since many people had fled the district and many of the vulnerable had already died, so that the removal of the handle cannot be said to have ended the epidemic by itself, a fact that Snow himself acknowledged, though he thought the pump had done its worst damage in the first few days.

The explanation for how the pump had become poisoned came from the local curate, Henry Whitehead, who had begun by thinking Snow mistaken and ended up as his closest ally, because his own door-to-door questioning among parishioners turned up the first case, a baby girl at 40 Broad Street who had fallen ill with diarrhoea in the last days of August and whose soiled napkins had been emptied into a cesspool a few feet from the well supplying the pump. When the well was later dug up an inspector found that the brickwork lining it was decayed and that waste from the cesspool could seep in.

The official committee that investigated the outbreak concluded that the evidence did not justify abandoning the miasma theory, and Snow died in 1858, aged only forty-five, without seeing his argument win. Acceptance came slowly over the following decades, helped along by the work of Whitehead, by London's later cholera epidemics, and finally by the identification of the cholera bacterium, first glimpsed by an Italian anatomist in the very year of the Soho outbreak and demonstrated convincingly by Robert Koch in 1883, after which Snow came to be regarded as one of the founders of modern epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations.
